title: An AI system is not just a single model
body: An AI system isn’t made up of just a single model. Actual services involve multiple stages, such as input preparation, searching, evidence selection, prompt generation, model invocation, output validation, log storage, and cost management. The model is merely the core component responsible for generating answers or making decisions. When reading code, don’t just look at the line that calls the model; to understand the overall structure, you must also examine what data is prepared beforehand and what validation is performed afterward. title: Prompt: Instructions for the model
body: A prompt is a set of instructions given to the model. While it can consist solely of a user’s question, in actual services, it often includes the model’s role, response format, prohibited actions, reference materials, and examples. A good prompt clearly tells the model what it should and should not do. When reading code, if the prompt is a long string, it should be treated as a critical setting for adjusting output quality. In RAG, retrieved evidence can also be included in the prompt. title: Context Window: The range the model can see at one time
body: The context window is the range of input that a model can process at one time. The user’s question, previous conversations, retrieved documents, and system prompts must all fall within this range for the model to reference them. If the scope is exceeded, some content must be truncated or summarized. Therefore, in AI apps that handle long documents, chunking, retrieval, summarization, and prioritization are crucial. When reading code, the context window must be considered in relation to the number of tokens, prompt length, and the number of search results. title: Chunking: Breaking Down Long Documents
body: Chunking is the process of dividing a long document into smaller pieces. Since models and search systems have difficulty handling documents that are too long all at once, they split them into paragraphs or sections and store and search them in that format. In RAG, chunks relevant to the query are identified and passed to the model. If the chunks are too large, irrelevant content may be included; if they are too small, the context may be disrupted. When reading code, you should verify how chunk size, overlap, and source text location information are managed. title: Fine-tuning: Changing the Model's Behavior
body: Fine-tuning is the process of further training a pre-trained model with additional data to adapt it to a specific task or style. Rather than rebuilding the model’s foundational knowledge from scratch, it is used to make the model better align with the desired output format or domain-specific conventions. If the data quality is low, the fine-tuning results may also suffer. title: LoRA: How to Perform Lightweight Fine-Tuning
body: LoRA is a method for tailoring a large model to a specific format or task by training only a small set of additional weights, without having to retrain the entire model. Training the entire model is costly and time-consuming, but LoRA allows for relatively lightweight experimentation. However, LoRA does not provide all the necessary knowledge from scratch, so data quality and the target format are crucial. When reading code, think of LoRA as an adapter that is added on top of the base model. title: Inference: The step of generating answers using the trained model
body: Inference is the process of using a trained model to generate actual answers or predictions. If training is the process of teaching the model, then inference is the process of feeding input into the trained model and receiving the results. When a chatbot answers a question or an image model classifies an image, that is also inference. When reading code, inference involves model loading, input preprocessing, prediction execution, and output postprocessing. Cost and latency also become important during the inference stage. title: Latency: The time it takes to receive a response
body: Latency is the time it takes for a response to be returned after a request is sent. In AI apps, model calls, searches, database queries, and network round-trip times all affect latency. If the response takes too long, users may feel as though the service has stopped working. That’s why techniques such as caching, short inputs, fast searches, and streaming output are used. When reading code, you should check the sections related to latency for any repetitive calls or unnecessarily time-consuming operations. title: Hallucination: A Plausible Wrong Answer
body: Hallucination is a phenomenon in which AI generates plausible but incorrect answers. While models are highly capable of constructing natural-sounding sentences, they do not always verify facts before responding. Therefore, important answers require supporting documents, search results, calculation results, and verification rules. In code, this is linked to structures such as retrieval, evidence check, confidence score, and validation. When reading AI responses, you should also check whether they are supported by evidence. title: Guardrail: A Safety Mechanism for AI Outputs
body: Guardrail is a safety mechanism for AI outputs. Since models can generate incorrect, dangerous, or unformatted answers, services implement safeguards such as prohibition rules, output validation, justification checks, and handling of follow-up questions. For example, in a learning app, rules can be set to restrict terminology that exceeds a student’s level or to provide hints rather than immediately revealing the correct answer. When reading code, Guardrail connects to the validation logic before and after the model.
